International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the era of U.S.
  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a upcoming top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.
  • Many travelers might not notice the difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a upcoming top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: fresh suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

It's part of airlines' massive bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," remarked Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt noted.

"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he stated. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

Industry observers note that its upcoming cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

Recent findings suggest that american Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 at the moment to somewhere in the 30s.

Sources indicate that "You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, noted in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

Recent findings suggest that first class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt stated. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

Recent findings suggest that there are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

Recent findings suggest that "I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month mentioned it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter mentioned last month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” now streaming on Prime Video.

In the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” the future of humanity is anything but certain.

Sources indicate that after discovering that the stolen memory they’ve spent the series searching for contains Dr. Eldon Tyrell’s (Joe Turkell) original Nexus-1 replicant design, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer) face off against Julius (Sam C. Wilson), whose plans to create a newly introduced generation of replicants threaten to reshape the future of both humans and replicants. Related Stories 'Ted' Animated Series Drops Foul-Mouthed, Pot-Filled First Trailer NBC News Will Cancel Streaming Show 'Stay Tuned,' Trim Some Positions in Staff Realignment.

According to recent reports, olwen ultimately kills Julius, but not before he destroys the memory containing the secrets to his original design. In a final twist, Olwen, who was living out the last few days of her pre-determined lifespan as a replicant, discovers she has been transformed into a Nexus-1 herself and can now live the longer life she wished for. Meanwhile, Cora learns that Helena (Sheila Atim), the woman who raised her and Elias (Lewis Gribben), was a replicant, forcing her to reconsider everything she previously believed about humanity and explore the possibility that humans and replicants aren’t so different after all.

According to recent reports, elias, on the other hand, a more radical approach. Determined to fight back against the replicants and reclaim societal control as humans, he broadcasts a message to the population of Los Angeles falsely claiming responsibility for destroying the replicant birthing center in hopes of sparking a human uprising (Julius was the one responsible). But there is no rebellion. The replicants are still in control, and Elias’ fate is unknown.

Cora returns the LAPD, where she undergoes another Index test overseen by Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey) — a parallel to the premiere episode in which the results revealed she possesses no empathy, despite being a human. This time, however, Cora has developed empathy after learning to care for Olwen, who is now jetting off-world.

Below, “Blade Runner 2099” creator Silka Luisa breaks down the finale and what it means for the future of replicants in the “Blade Runner” universe.

In a recent development, oh my gosh! What did you think? I’m so curious. What did you understand? What didn’t you understand?

Sources indicate that exactly. We had a lot of conversations about, “Should we change their costume? Should we make it clear who is what?” But what makes the world so unsettling is that you never really know, and I love that about the films. It was really important to us that you were never really on firm ground there.

That’s so gratifying, because so many early conversations were had about how we make this accessible for people that haven’t seen one of the films, both of the films or read the book. We had to find an entry point with original characters that you’re also not going to have to catch everybody up to a bunch of lore.

In a recent development, yeah. Sorry. At the end of the day, it’s noir. It’s not a revolution story, and that’s why it was so important with the Elias storyline to give this sense of, “Is there going to be a rebellion? Is there going to be an uprising?” No. It’s really just capitalism, and you’re in a noir world where no one is coming to save you. This is the status quo, and you have to carve out your own future within these new circumstances.

Elias’ story is about someone who is really just trying to find agency. At the beginning of the season, he’s taken care of by his sister, which is beautiful, but is very claustrophobic. And then he thinks that there’s going to be some kind of uprising, and they’re going to be able to recreate the world that once was. The truth is that that’s not what’s going to happen, and there’s no one coming to save the day for him. While that is deflating, it’s also an opportunity for him to falsely claim that he did this act of terrorism, because the truth is, if you want change in the world, sometimes you have to be the spark that ignites it. And it was really just trying to find a moment in the sun for him too, so that he could really be the change or be the hope for change that he wanted.

Sources indicate that it’s the same as with “[Blade Runner] 2049,” where I was like, “I think this is what happens four months later.” I’m sure everyone had different ideas. I obviously have my own story for each character and how I imagine it will continue, but there’s definitely a reason we cut the rope at the points we did.

In a recent development, that test has been an evolution through the films. In the first film, there’s a void comp test, which is a straight up empathy test to tell the difference between replicant and human. In “2049,” there’s a baseline test, which measures emotional stability to see if you’re able to be a police officer.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve blended those, because now that replicants are policing the human population, there’s a risk that they could develop empathy. If they develop empathy, it makes it harder to put intubating bags over them and police them, and you don’t want that.

Industry observers note that it was an vital mirror scene to the end of the pilot, where she essentially passes that test, meaning she doesn’t have any empathy. So she is a human who’s just been stripped of her humanity, and I think that if empathy is the distinction between replicant and human, it’s so interesting, because it is not definitive. It’s something that you can gain or lose.

Recent findings suggest that and at the beginning of this series, she lost it. Then at the end through this connection with Olwen, she rediscovers it.

Recent findings suggest that yeah. I think Cora has lost her own mother figure in Helena, and the surprise of the season for her is that she finds the surrogate mother in Olwen at the end.

I knew we wanted to end on a glimpse of off-world, which, if you’re a fan, has been very mythologized. We wanted to give a little peek of what it could be, but trying to find some hope in the ending.

Sources indicate that exactly. And the endings of the films are ambiguous. They don’t give you definitive answers, and there’s been a lot of debate about both of them, even in the writers’ room, about how we all understood certain final moments, which is always so much fun because I think that it just shows you that everyone is having an engaged and personal experience of the material. That was really what we were trying to strike that balance: how do we make this feel conclusive enough so that people know we have given them a true ending, but at the same time honor the films and leave enough questions for people to debate?

It’s a tragedy, in this sense where they never get to have a forever ever together. She tells Cora to shoot on sight, and she does. And I think that she doesn’t really believe him when he’s saying why he left her. I wanted her storyline and her romance to actually be a very human romance. She’s really a wounded lover who’s been left in her final days, and she doesn’t understand why. And the real emotional reason she’s searching for answers is, she wants to understand why she was abandoned.

Industry observers note that in the lore, they don’t give you a lot of details about what Tyrell’s original intentions were and the original different models. That always seemed intentional. So, when you think about Tyrell as a character, he’s so grand in the first film, and he’s such a dreamer. He seems so poetic. It just doesn’t seem like he would have created these beings to be something small and just for labor, and that never really made sense to me from who he was. Those two things didn’t seem like they fit, and so I was thinking, “What was his original intention when he made replicants?” He seems to have such a God complex. He would really want to create what comes next, the “next us.” And that is something that is better than us. It’s not smaller. It doesn’t have smaller lifespans. It’s meant to go further. It’s meant to extend far beyond.

Industry observers note that no. The end of “2049” gives you the sense that there is a possibility of a mutiny brewing, and my own mind as an audience member was just like, “Oh, well, they’re going to uprise.” That’s what I assumed happened, and so that was how I filled in the gap personally. And this is really just in the aftermath of what that would look like.

Sources indicate that it’s been part of the conversation for a couple years now, and I think it’s obviously coming to a head with all of the AI debate, because we really are having a mirror held up to us, and we’re starting to ask, “What is the value of humans? What can we do that nothing else can do? What is our purpose if we don’t work right?” All these massive philosophical questions are being forced upon us, so it’s a really intense moment to be alive. Growing up, I never had this fear that humanity could ever end. That there would be a passing of the baton to something else, and it’s been in the zeitgeist. That was definitely in my mind as I started the project.

If you’re going to ask the question of, “What does it mean to be human?,” it does make sense to want to have more points of view on that, and that definitely felt like an addition to the conversation.

Recent findings suggest that that was probably one of my favorite sets and sequences in the series. I just love the idea that, even though replicants have power, they still have this longing for what they can’t have. It was so fun to build that out. We looked at a lot of real-world references from ’70s New York and real peep demonstrates, and the coin is taken from the real slots that they would have. There’s so many fun details in world building. You have this concept which is just prosthetics. How would you have that? How would you actually try and assimilate that in this kind of grungy underworld? The idea that you never get to grow old with someone is when Olwen emotionally realizes that her life has been cut so short.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.
  • "The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu, who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey, to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.
  • Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.

"The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu, who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey, to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.

Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts. This includes extreme weather events such as floods, heat waves and wildfires as well as slow-onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification and damage to infrastructure and crops.

In a recent development, but the fund is already struggling to meet demand. It received $2.8 billion (€2.56 billion) in urgent requests in a first call for funding, with only $342 million available at the time.

Even the money promised has not fully arrived. Only about half of the money right now pledged had been received by this summer.

While the European Commission signed a €25 million ($27 million) contribution agreement to the fund on the margins of COP31, formalizing an earlier pledge made at COP28, and Spain pledged an additional €15 million, other contributions to loss and damage remained scarce.

The fund's first emergency response is going to be paid out to Nepal. The board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had provisionally set aside $21.6 million following the catastrophic glacier collapse that triggered flash floods in August, killing more than 1,500 people with 5,600 more missing.

Recent findings suggest that but the money has not moved yet. Nepal must first submit a funding request setting out how it will be spent.

"It's asking for a country that is dealing with the climate emergency to work on a proposal," Nepali climate finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel noted, adding a layer of bureaucracy inefficient to address the urgency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, nepal is already waiting on another request, filed after floods in Kathmandu and landslides in the eastern hills. "There's already one pending proposal sitting on the table," Kandel noted. Unless the fund speeds up, he warned, it's "going to disappoint many, many countries.".

Pakistan which led the push for the fund in 2022 after floods affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, also hasn't seen any of the money yet.

"Pakistan was one of the countries which really spoke up and managed to get the loss and damage fund on the climate agenda. But it takes a long time," Pakistan's Minister of State for Climate Change, Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, told DW.

According to recent reports, "We have still not really got anything. We haven't seen anything on the ground at all as yet," Kharal said. Pakistan has submitted two projects and was told the cap is $200 million.

Other forms of aid often come in the form of loans.

"These promises, they are hollow promises," mentioned Abid Qaiyum Suleri, Executive Director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad, adding that for a heavily indebted country, the form of the money matters as much as the amount.

"We do not want that a climate disaster in Pakistan should translate into further debt for Pakistan," Kharal stated, calling for grants rather than loans.

Industry News: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming genetic findings reveal that marine animals living deep beneath the surface of the Gulf may be at greater risk of extinction than scientists once thought.
  • As biodiversity declines around the world, the deep ocean has largely been regarded as a natural sanctuary where marine life is better protected from environmental threats.
  • Industry observers note that drawing on 12 years of genetic data, researchers identified concerning signs of extinction risk in five marine species that inhabit waters hundreds of meters below the surface of the Gulf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming genetic findings reveal that marine animals living deep beneath the surface of the Gulf may be at greater risk of extinction than scientists once thought.

As biodiversity declines around the world, the deep ocean has largely been regarded as a natural sanctuary where marine life is better protected from environmental threats. However, new research led by scientists at Florida International University (FIU) is challenging that assumption.

Industry observers note that drawing on 12 years of genetic data, researchers identified concerning signs of extinction risk in five marine species that inhabit waters hundreds of meters below the surface of the Gulf. Their findings suggest that a biodiversity crisis may also be developing in one of Earth's most extensive and poorly understood environments.

Recent findings suggest that the research was led by FIU marine scientist Pedro A. Peres of the Bracken-Grissom Lab and focused on three species of lanternfish and two species of deep-sea shrimp collected between 2011 and 2023.

It has been revealed that the team examined DNA from 486 specimens to determine how the populations have changed over time and assess their ability to withstand future environmental stress. According to Peres, few studies have investigated changes in the genetic makeup of deep-sea animals over an extended period.

Hidden Genetic Signs of Extinction Risk.

Every species examined displayed genetic characteristics linked to a greater risk of extinction, Peres noted. One species of lanternfish, Diaphus dumerilii, experienced an approximately 8% reduction in genetic diversity in just 12 years. This loss matches or exceeds declines recorded in some threatened and endangered animals across considerably longer timespans.

In a recent development, all five species also had relatively small effective population sizes. Rather than indicating that the animals are necessarily scarce, this finding suggests that only a limited proportion of individuals are passing their genetic information on to subsequent generations.

Industry observers note that "This challenges the idea that deep-sea species are naturally more resilient because they occupy such vast environments," Peres said. "It demonstrates how much we can miss when we look only at population abundance without considering their genetic diversity and long-term viability.".

Sources indicate that genetic variation plays a fundamental role in determining whether a species can survive environmental changes, explained Heather Bracken-Grissom, assistant director of the Institute of Environment's Coastlines and Oceans Division. Bracken-Grissom, a co-author of the study, has led research exploring the genetic health and resilience of animals living in the deep ocean.

"Genetic diversity provides the variation populations need to adapt to changing conditions, resist disease and recover from environmental disturbances," she remarked. "When that diversity disappears, a species can also lose the ability to withstand future threats.".

Climate Change Could Dramatically Shrink Deep-Sea Habitats.

Sources indicate that the team also used climate models to estimate how environmental conditions in the Gulf could affect the availability of suitable deep-sea habitats by 2050 and 2100. The projections indicate that four of the five species could face substantial habitat losses, potentially reaching 70%.

Peres noted that these results are especially troubling given the longstanding belief that the enormous habitats and widespread geographic distributions of deep-sea animals allow them to maintain large, resilient populations.

The discoveries also prompt fresh questions about the long-term environmental impact of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Earlier research revealed considerable reductions in deep-sea animal populations in the aftermath of the disaster.

While the scientists have not established a direct link between the oil spill and the genetic changes they observed, their results indicate that environmental disruptions could have repercussions extending well beyond their initial impact.

Recent findings suggest that "Our results suggest some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill," Peres remarked. "This has important implications for understanding the consequences of environmental disturbances. Events such as oil spills may affect populations that already have limited genetic resilience.".

An Urgent Need To Monitor Deep-Sea Biodiversity.

The study, which also includes co-authors Keith Sellers of FIU and Tracey T. Sutton of Nova Southeastern University, highlights the importance of examining the genetic health of marine populations. Monitoring changes in DNA over time could help scientists identify threats to species survival that conventional population surveys fail to detect.

"This study serves as a wake-up call for the scientific community," Peres said, "highlighting the urgent need to integrate genetic monitoring into biodiversity assessments and emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring to better understand and detect changes in marine populations over time.".

The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • It has been revealed that wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

It has been revealed that wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had rolled out aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a latest class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

“It’s so much more than the four names that have been confirmed,” Glover remarked during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

Glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

It has been revealed that koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

The Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

According to recent reports, if all goes to proposal, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton mentioned via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

According to recent reports, the Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already stated delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

According to recent reports, vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

It has been revealed that “I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch remarked in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

It has been revealed that “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch mentioned. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She stated the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

In a recent development, “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

  • More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea.
  • The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX.
  • It has been revealed that "Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

It has been revealed that "Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond.".

Life thrives in extreme underwater lakes.

Brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.

Recent findings suggest that "We were very lucky," noted Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project.".

Hidden records of ancient tsunamis and earthquakes.

Industry observers note that beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

In a recent development, earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have notable implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The study, titled "Discovery of the deep-sea NEOM Brine Pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea," was published on June 27, 2022, in Communications Earth & Environment.

Industry observers note that the research team included Sam J. Purkis, Hannah Shernisky, Peter K. Swart, Arash Sharifi, Amanda Oehlert, Gaëlle Duchâtellier, James Klaus, Gregor P. Eberli, Larry Peterson, and Graham Kolodziej from the UM Rosenstiel School; Fabio Marchese and Francesca Benzoni from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Red Sea Research Center; Giovanni Chimienti from the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy; Andrew Craig and Mattie Rodrigue from OceanX; Jürgen Titschack from MARUM -- Center for Marine Environmental Sciences in Germany; and Ameer Abdulla from NEOM.

NEOM, a company developing the Saudi Arabian coastline, provided funding for the four-week research expedition aboard the OceanXplorer.

Watch the NEOM OceanX documentary about the discovery: https://youtu.be/bWNftnYDx9c.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.
  • Industry observers note that "I have long had three goals," he remarked.
  • Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.

Industry observers note that "I have long had three goals," he remarked. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home.".

Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.

The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.

This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.

"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," said former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.

"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision.".

Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.

In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.

"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person.".

This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.

"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director noted.

"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition.".

It has been revealed that on the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.

In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.

According to recent reports, this, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.

Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

#139208. For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1280 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that even before a new neuroscience study appeared in Nature, its preliminary version had been downloaded more than 11,000 times.
  • Do neurons operate like individual tools, such as hammers and saws, each designed for a particular job?
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute examined an extensive collection of mouse brain recordings gathered through an international collaboration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that even before a new neuroscience study appeared in Nature, its preliminary version had been downloaded more than 11,000 times. The research addresses one of the oldest and most hotly debated questions in neuroscience: how specialized are the individual cells that make up the brain?

Do neurons operate like individual tools, such as hammers and saws, each designed for a particular job? Or are they more like Swiss Army knives, capable of handling many different tasks?

Recent findings suggest that researchers at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute examined an extensive collection of mouse brain recordings gathered through an international collaboration. Their analysis revealed that while some neurons are indeed specialists, most appear capable of responding to many different kinds of information.

"We have to move away from this image of the brain as a machine made of gears, with every gear having an exact purpose that we can attach a label to," said Stefano Fusi, PhD, a principal investigator at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute, a member of the Kavli Institute for Brain Science and the paper's co-senior author. "The brain doesn't work like that. Instead, most neurons can display a huge diversity of responses, and this can help the brain solve a huge number of different tasks.".

The discovery could help explain how the brain achieves its remarkable ability to perform complex tasks. It could also provide a foundation for understanding what happens when brain function is disrupted and identifying ways to restore it.

Revisiting a Decades-Old Neuroscience Debate.

Industry observers note that the question of whether neurons are specialists or generalists "is an old, notable question, and one which researchers have really strong opinions on," said Lorenzo Posani, PhD, the study's co-lead author and a principal investigator at the Paris Brain Institute and France's CNRS. Posani conducted the research while working at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute.

In a recent development, scientists have long known that the brain contains distinct regions responsible for functions such as sight and smell. This organization suggests that individual neurons might also have narrowly defined roles. However, the brain is also an extraordinarily powerful biological computer capable of adapting to countless situations, raising the possibility that its individual neurons are similarly versatile.

In a recent development, one reason the debate has persisted is that researchers have approached the question under widely different experimental conditions, Posani explained. Previous studies examined different animal species, investigated different parts of the brain, or required animals to complete different activities. Unsurprisingly, their conclusions often conflicted. Some experiments identified highly specialized neurons, while others revealed cells with much broader capabilities.

A Massive Study of 43 Brain Regions.

To obtain a more consistent picture of neural activity, the researchers focused exclusively on mice performing the same type of task. They also examined numerous brain regions simultaneously, drawing on datasets considerably larger than those typically used in neuroscience research.

The recordings, collected by the International Brain Laboratory consortium, captured the activity of individual neurons across 43 regions of the mouse cerebral cortex.

The analysis revealed an vital distinction. Neurons in primary sensory regions, including areas responsible for processing visual information, tended to exhibit more specialized responses. Across other regions, however, individual neurons displayed a considerably wider range of activity. The overall findings suggest that generalists, rather than specialists, dominate much of the cortex.

According to recent reports, "We're not saying that there are no specialized neurons," mentioned Dr. Fusi, who is also a professor of neuroscience at Columbia's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons and a member of Columbia's Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. "We're saying they are the exceptions. They're not the rule.".

Most Neurons Are Versatile in Different Ways.

Despite the versatility of individual neurons, the brain retains a distinct regional organization. By examining how a neuron responded during a particular task, the scientists could identify with surprising accuracy which functional module it belonged to. Yet membership in a particular brain module did not generally mean that a neuron was limited to a single function.

In a recent development, "For example, compare this to maps of voter opinions," Dr. Posani said. "There are clear clusters where people generally vote the same way. But when you zoom in, you see mixes of opinions.".

In a recent development, the researchers also uncovered another striking feature of neural activity. Not only do most neurons handle multiple kinds of information, but their patterns of activity rarely mirror those of other neurons.

According to recent reports, "Each is versatile in its own way," states study co-lead author Shuqi Wang, a doctoral student at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland. According to Wang, this diversity helps give the brain its flexibility and impressive computational abilities.

The Secret Behind the Brain's Computing Power.

In a recent development, the researchers propose that the versatility of neurons allows individual brain cells to represent several types of information at once. For example, a neuron might respond to both the color of an object, such as red or black, and its shape, such as a circle or square.

Sources indicate that working together, groups of neurons can form what scientists call "high-dimensional" representations of information. These representations capture multiple characteristics simultaneously, allowing the brain to distinguish a red circle from a black square, for instance.

According to recent reports, this arrangement gives groups of neurons considerable flexibility in how they process incoming information and generate responses. Rather than requiring an entirely separate neural representation for every new task, the brain can draw on existing combinations of neural activity.

Recent findings suggest that "You can reuse these high-dimensional representations for lots of different tasks," Dr. Fusi said.

Rethinking How Scientists Study the Brain.

According to recent reports, the findings also have significant implications for how neuroscientists investigate brain function. Because a single neuron can carry information about several different variables, determining precisely what it represents by examining its activity alone can be extremely difficult.

A clearer picture emerges when scientists analyze the combined activity of many neurons, much as the brain itself processes information through populations of cells.

Recent findings suggest that this represents an notable change in perspective for the neuroscience community, "which for decades focused on one neuron at a time, discarding all neurons whose responses could not be understood," Dr. Fusi said.

Do Human Brain Cells Work the Same Way?

The researchers are now collaborating with Ueli Rutishauser's research group at Caltech to determine whether human neurons exhibit similar patterns of versatility.

They also hope to establish whether the degree of specialization among neurons changes depending on the particular demands of a task.

"There is still a lot to discover," Dr. Fusi stated.

The paper, "Rarely categorical and highly separable: how neural representations change along the cortical hierarchy," was published in Nature.

Recent findings suggest that the full list of authors includes Lorenzo Posani, Shuqi Wang, Samuel P. Muscinelli, Liam Paninski and Stefano Fusi.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (RF1AG080818, U19NS123716), the Simons Foundation, the Kavli Foundation, the Gatsby Foundation (GAT3708), and the Swartz Foundation. Additional support was provided by the National Science Foundation and the DoD Office of the Under Secretary of Defense (R&E) under Cooperative Agreement PHY-2229929 (the NSF AI Institute for Artificial and Natural Intelligence). Dr. Posani received additional support through the NIH 1K99MH135166-01 grant.

Materials provided by The Zuckerman Institute at Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
