💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, first there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya.
  • Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
  • What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, first there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.

Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.

What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.

And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

In a recent development, furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.

Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet.".

According to recent reports, ukrainian special forces are also noted to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.

Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

According to recent reports, "Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war.".

Recent findings suggest that officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising.".

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.".

She mentioned about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.

According to recent reports, she added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody.".

This article was originally written in German.

Last week, international health authorities formally revealed that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

Recent findings suggest that the national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

According to recent reports, on November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department confirmed its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. Fresh York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.

The virus isn’t slowing down. Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in the air for up to two hours. Up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will fall ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they’ve been vaccinated or previously infected. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible people is only growing.

According to recent reports, to keep measles from getting a foothold in a community, vaccination rates need to be 95 percent or higher. According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. But even in those states, there are pockets and communities that are undervaccinated.

In Pennsylvania, which has the record for the largest measles outbreak this year so far, the epidemic curve appears to be past the peak. But Wisconsin seems to be in the thick of its outbreak. As of today, the state case count hit 920, with 88 cases reported since November 20. The health department has tallied 418 cases since the start of the month.

In most cases, measles causes high fever, a telltale rash, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. But some develop complications, which can be severe and even life-threatening, including pneumonia and brain swelling, which can result in intellectual disabilities and hearing loss. In pregnant people, measles can cause more severe illness and pregnancy complications, including premature birth, low birth weight, and congenital measles.

After an acute infection, every person infected faces a long immune recovery in which they are newly vulnerable to a slew of other diseases. The measles virus specifically infects and destroys memory immune cells, which hold molecular records of germs the immune system has previously encountered and defeated. In other words, the immunity built up over the person’s life gets wiped, a phenomenon called immune amnesia. A study in 2019 estimated that the measles virus erases up to 73 percent of a person’s antibody repertoire, which would otherwise defend against infections and reinfections. To regain protection, people must be exposed to the germs again, either through reinfections or repeat vaccinations.

People who appear to recover are also at risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare but devastating condition in which the virus remains in the central nervous system, striking years later to cause a progressive, fatal neurological disease.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday stated it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.
  • Sources indicate that it identified the men as Mostafa Al-R.
  • Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday stated it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.

Sources indicate that it identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and stated that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne, several hours' drive to the north.

Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.

Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.

Sources indicate that after two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X.

Sources indicate that "Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added.

Prosecutors stated the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.

According to recent reports, they remarked that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran.

Sources indicate that mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025.".

Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks.".

"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The proposal was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out.".

Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency, the BfV.

More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.

Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.

One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.

The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.

These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9, which caused property damage but no injuries.

In a recent development, police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later. An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after, prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.

In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March, not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.

Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

Below is a roundup of the top news stories from Germany from Thursday, November 26, 2026:.

Michael Noetzel, the new justice minister in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, has come under fire for a now-deleted social media post promoting the far-left antifa.

The controversy centers on a photo of Noetzel wearing a T-shirt with the historic 1932 antifa logo and raising his left fist.

Noetzel, a representative of the socialist Left Party, also wrote that it is vital for young people to attend antifa meetings.

Philipp Amthor, who serves as acting head of the state chapter of the conservative CDU, demanded that Noetzel "make an unambiguous statement now regarding his position on left-wing extremist and violence-prone groups within the antifa scene.".

Enrico Schult, who is a parliamentary group leader of the far-right populist AfD, mentioned: "If you have such a hard time distancing yourself from violent structures, then you are unfit to serve as minister of justice.".

The ministry stated that Noetzel "naturally takes a clear stand against extremism.".

The ministry also identified right-wing extremism as the greatest threat to democracy and that combating it is a priority.

The German government intends to acquire a stake in the Canada-based artificial intelligence technology firm Cohere for the symbolic sum of €1.

The Digital Ministry confirmed media reports that the Finance Ministry had approved the government's small stake in the multinational company.

According to a ministry spokesperson, the government is presently considering investing a larger sum.

Cohere would commit itself "to helping increase competitiveness in AI in Germany and to securing jobs, research and development and investment in Germany," the spokesperson stated.

He added that the German government would receive "specific governance guarantees that safeguard the goal of digital sovereignty.".

Cohere's goal is to develop sovereign AI services for the public administration, as well as finance, defense, energy, telecommunications, and healthcare.

This technology is designed to operate independently of major US data center operators.

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman charged with spying for Russia began in Berlin.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court noted.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses.

Recent findings suggest that several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

Read more about the charges against the woman, as well as the diplomatic fallout caused by the case.

IG Metall, representing millions of workers in Germany's metal and electrical industry, is the country's largest trade union.

The deal came after more than 24 hours of talks with employers.

Read the full story on what the union and industry leaders agreed to.

Germany national player Laura Freigang has been banned from playing until October 7, 2027, over three doping tests she missed, meaning that she will not be available to participate in the World Cup in Brazil next year, the German Football Federation (DFB) remarked in a statement on Thursday.

The ban comes amid a settlement between Freigang, 28, who is also the captain of Frankfurt Eintracht, and the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA).

Freigang has been the subject of proceedings for several months, having been accused of not being at the location she specified for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.

In June, she stated that the missed tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to revision in the system on a daily and hourly basis.".

Freigang has played 45 times for Germany, scoring 17 goals.

However, she has not recently been a regular in the team.

Read the full story on why Freigang will miss the 2027 World Cup.

The archdiocese in the western city of Cologne was ordered on Wednesday to pay a woman who was sexually abused by a priest for years €550,000 ($601,865) in damages — the highest amount a German court has ever awarded to a victim of abuse in theCatholic Church.

That amount will, however, by offset by the €360,000 that the Catholic Church's Independent Commission for Recognition Payments has already paid to the claimant.

The woman had previously had her claim rejected by the Cologne Regional Court, which, although it accepted that the victim had been severely sexually abused by a priest in the 1970s and 1980s, argued that the archdiocese could not be made responsible for the crimes because the man had acted "more or less as a private individual.".

The higher regional court has now overturned that ruling at an appeal, saying that the priest had approached the claimant "under the cover of his church work" when he was a deacon.

It noted he used his standing in the church to be allowed to take in foster children, of whom the claimant was one.

The priest was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2022.

German Foreign MinisterJohann Wadephul has warned against an expansion of the Ukraine conflict into other regions after the Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in Libya.

"Ukraine's ​right to self-defense is undisputed and we ​do support Ukraine, but I strongly ⁠warn ​against allowing ​this conflict to spread ​geographically," he ‌said at ​a ⁠press conference in Berlin with ⁠his ​Romanian counterpart Dan Neculaescu.

Wadephul also condemned reported Russian attacks on two foreign freight ships said to be carrying grain near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, saying such attacks did not concern only the security of nearby nations but also the food security of people in the Global South.

Sources indicate that "It is clear that we cannot accept drone attacks on trading vessels," he said. "NATO will therefore step up its engagement in the region.".

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has called for closer economic and political partnerships with African countries as he wound up what was probably his last trip to the continent as head of state.

Speaking in Kenya, Steinmeier stated that there were great variations in the state of development between individual countries and even within some of them.

"But I believe it is worthwhile investing in Africa and in relations with African countries," he noted.

He said this was not just meant with a view to possible investment by German companies drawn by Africa's mostly young national populations and developing markets. "That is true, but we should not limit our view to that. Many African countries now have political weight and growing self-confidence and want a say in shaping the future of the world," he said. "Africa, it has become clear, is a continent that requires patience if you want to discover it," Steinmeier said. "There is no single Africa, but very many.".

Before Kenya, Steinmeier visited Ivory Coast and Ghana. On the final day of his trip, he went to the Crescent Island nature reserve on Lake Naivasha, an area under threat from climate change.

Chocolate manufacturers in Germany produced less in 2025 than the year before.

According to figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) released on Thursday, around 1 million metric tons (1.1 US tons) of chocolate products containing cocoa were made in Germany in 2025, compared with 1.1 million tons in 2024.

This represents a reduction of 5.7%.

Much of the chocolate produced in Germany is exported (916,200 tons in 2025), while considerable amounts are also imported (530,000 tons in 2025), with a quarter of that amount coming from neighboring Belgium.

Altogether 13.4% of exports went to France, followed by Poland (9.6%) and the UK (9.3%).

According to Destatis, citing the EU's statistical agency Eurostat, Germany remains the European leader in the production of gingerbread, or Lebkuchen, manufacturing 39.4% of the entire EU supply of the sweet treat, compared with Poland on 17.3% and the Netherlands on 17%.

German authorities say that two Iraqi citizens believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group have been arrested on suspicion of having planned a number of anti-Jewish attacks, including on a synagogue in the western city of Cologne.

You can read more about the arrests and the charges laid against the two men in our article: Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack.

A survey by police union GdP has shown that some 69% of police in Germany are in favor of a ban on private fireworks on Newly introduced Year's Eve.

According to the survey of 9,000 members, more than 70% feel that the situation for police on the evening would improve if such a ban were in place.

Altogether 54% of respondents who had been on duty during the past 10 years of Upcoming Year's Eve festivities reported having been in a dangerous or threatening situation caused by fireworks.

A whole 195 respondents noted they had been injured by fireworks on the evening.

Industry observers note that the poll was prompted by an open letter to Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt by a group calling itself #böllerciao (Goodbye firecrackers) with some 1.17 million signatories. The name is a play on the famous anti-Nazi song Bella Ciao.

The group includes 86 organizations, among them Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and the GdP, who have called for a ban on private fireworks to protect people, emergency personnel, animals and the environment.

Plans foreseeing a rise of €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in the budget for the Interior Ministry have been approved by the three parties in Germany's coalition government, after much debate centering on something that makes up a relatively small proportion of that money: the controversial planned centers for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

According to Klaus-Peter Willsch of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), just €5 million are earmarked for the so-called return hubs, shared between several European countries.

He stated the €20 million that has often been cited as being for the Rwanda migration centers was not only for the hubs in that country, but for other potential projects in third countries as well.

Despite the relatively small amounts of money involved, the Rwanda intends devised by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) along with Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece came under fire not only from coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) but particularly from opposition parties.

The Green Party and the Left Party both rejected the idea for ethical reasons, with Green lawmaker Leon Eckert speaking of "state-organized human trafficking," while Dietmar Bartsch of the Left pointed out that the deal was being made with an authoritarian regime.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), for its part, noted it found the aims too soft, with parliamentarian Marcus Bühl calling them a "smoke screen," as just 20 rejected asylum-seekers from Germany were to be initially sent to Rwanda under the scheme.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that dobrindt defended the scheme, saying that the opposition was trying to stir up controversy about a concept that had been approved at European level. He also called criticism of the political system in Rwanda inappropriate, citing a school for Afghan girls that had been set up in the country amid the ban on secondary education for females by the Taliban government.

The interior minister also praised the additional funds given to his ministry as a contribution to Germany's defense against hybrid attacks from Russia, with a rise in the budgets of both the IT security and the civic protection departments.

The draft 2027 budget, which was approved by the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the SPD, however includes less funding for the BAMF migration authority (from €999 million in 2026 to €994 million) and for integration aid for migrants and refugees (down €328 million to €1.07 billion).

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman due to go on trial on Thursday on charges of spying for Russia was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court noted.

It was not clear whether her trial could go ahead as planned.

The 57-year-old woman has been accused of passing information to an officer from Russia's GRU intelligence agency who was posing as a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Berlin.

Prosecutors allege that she used contacts with  current and former German Defense Ministry officials to collect information on military aid for Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry.

She also faces accusation of having provided her alleged handler access to key political events in Berlin.

The woman was arrested in late January, with the alleged involvement of the Russian Embassy causing considerable outrage in Berlin.

Russia's ambassador was summoned over the incident, and the handler — identified by news weekly Der Spiegel as the embassy's deputy military attache — was expelled from Germany.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The Bundestag is conducting its concluding debates on the budget for 2027 ahead of a final vote scheduled for Friday.

On Thursday, the focus will initially be on the individual budget for the Interior Ministry led by Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

The government foresees that the ministry, which is responsible for the federal police and the domestic intelligence agency BfV, among other things, will receive some €16.8 billion in 2027 ($18.43 billion), around €1 billion more than this year.

Lawmakers will then go on to debate the individual budgets for the Economics and Energy Ministry, the Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.

Opening the debates on Wednesday, Merz described the tight budget as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" — that Germany finds itself in.

"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

You can read more about what the planned record-breaking German budget for 2027 includes in this DW article:€561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink.

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn!

The second-to-last day of debates on Germany's 2027 budget, which foresees both record spending and borrowing, is getting underway in the parliament.

Lawmakers are being forced to grapple with a horde of economic and geopolitical challenges as they seek to set the right priorities, with an ideological split in the ruling coalition likely to bring additional heat to the discussions.

In other news, the trial is opening in Berlin of a woman accused of spying for Russia against the background of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And chocolate production went down in Germany last year, while the country remains the European leader in another Christmas specialty, gingerbread or Lebkuchen.

Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.
  • A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.
  • Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases.".

He tied improvement to the firm's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

The organization also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

Industry observers note that at Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart mentioned "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good.".

She similarly pointed to new products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

In a recent development, target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often.".

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the manufacturer has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

It has been revealed that michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and company-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

"Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker mentioned. His analysis indicated retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

Sources indicate that dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

Industry observers note that "Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," mentioned Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the tech giant's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need.".

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the company mentioned.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source noted, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person remarked, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source noted, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person remarked, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical upcoming insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have stated.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official stated in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Recent findings suggest that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, stated at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

In a recent development, the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

In a recent development, still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it.
  • Industry observers note that the Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

Recent findings suggest that it’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

Industry observers note that the Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most key problems in the field.”.

It has been revealed that the proof of the hypothesis was revealed by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already newly introduced and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

Recent findings suggest that but it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

It’s vital to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

Sources indicate that but AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

According to recent reports, AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

Sources indicate that mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

Sources indicate that but that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see newly introduced ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.

By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of fresh ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.

Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce upcoming insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

How mathematicians are expected to identify upcoming challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

Industry observers note that this is all new and progressing incredibly rapidly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.

But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

Recent findings suggest that there are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An crucial note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, mentioned in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

According to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they said the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

In a recent development, the Transport Ministry remarked the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency proposal at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he stated the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

#139118. Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.
  • In a recent development, the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop.
  • That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.

In a recent development, the shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.

That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials.

"I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality.".

It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen stated. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.

They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.

Industry observers note that for Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she notes will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.

Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added.

"It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said.

In a recent development, roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, stated she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated.

"It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she stated. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year.".

The trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.

Industry observers note that in October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation.

"You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive.".

And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.

Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed stated secondhand products offer better value than brand latest ones.

Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one.

"I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved.".

Industry observers note that according to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.

Iannone stated he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year.

"It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he mentioned.

At a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.

That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too.

"Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The firm's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece.

"To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.

It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem stated — something unique.

That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too.

"Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds.".

Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen noted. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.

Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date.

Industry observers note that "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen stated. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze.

It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.

At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It has been revealed that it was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.

"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.

When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.

She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.

It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, mentioned the report.

"It was ferociousâ¦ I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.

She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.

The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.

"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".

"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.

Sources indicate that "He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way.".

Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.

She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.

"All three of my children adored my husbandâ¦ He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh.".

Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source).

In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.

In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

In a recent development, like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; Â£32.4m).

It has been revealed that residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.

Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.

The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.

The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades.

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.

All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.

It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.

ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

Industry observers note that but for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.

Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire.

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, notes her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.

She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she claims that is at least of some consolation to her.

According to recent reports, "My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very leastâ¦ his suffering was minimal.".

Industry observers note that christy claims her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.

Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.

Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.

He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.

"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.

Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she notes, and channels her emotions through art.

She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.

Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.

Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management firm hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.

Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.

Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.

The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety concerns and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the tragedy the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction firm had a clean record.

Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.

In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.

Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.

It has been revealed that "I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," remarked Mrs Lau.

The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home.

Recent findings suggest that her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.

It has been revealed that "Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," mentioned Mrs Lau.

Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a latest house.

The government has said it will spend $867m (Â£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.

Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she stated.

"Should I say that we are fortunate?

In a recent development, "I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. ".

Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.

The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father.

As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".

"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she notes. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'".

It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.

"Every day, something reminds me of him," she mentioned.

Industry observers note that "I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are goneâ¦. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for customers worldwide.
  • Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online.
  • Recent findings suggest that the memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for customers worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

Amanda Silver, a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”.

In a recent development, microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling. As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft aims to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more rapidly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.

It has been revealed that microsoft has set targets of a one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”.
